props.title: Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow
props.initialSlug: Three tales of love across Italian social classes

sections.content: Vittorio De Sica's Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow (1963) represents the pinnacle of Italian comedy-anthology filmmaking, showcasing Sophia Loren and Marcello Mastroianni at their most magnetic. The film's three distinct stories capture different facets of Italian society - from Naples' working class to Milan's haute bourgeoisie to Rome's religious tensions. Each segment sparkles with De Sica's signature mix of neorealist touches and sophisticated comedy, following the tradition of earlier anthology films like L'Amore in Città (1953) and Boccaccio '70 (1962).

sections.content: The film's influence rippled through Italian cinema, establishing a template for sophisticated comedy that balanced social commentary with star power. Later works like The Easy Life (1962) and Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow would follow this model. De Sica, who had pioneered Italian Neorealism with Bicycle Thieves (1948), proves equally adept at comedy, never losing his keen eye for social observation even in lighter fare.

The Loren-Mastroianni pairing reached its creative peak here, their chemistry electric across all three segments. Their collaboration would continue through classics like Marriage Italian Style (1964) and Sunflower (1970), but never with quite the same magical combination of comedy and pathos. The famous striptease scene in the final segment became iconic, inspiring homages in films like Ready to Wear (1994). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Italian Comedy

sections.content: De Sica's film marks a crucial transition in Italian cinema from the stark neorealism of the post-war period to the more commercially viable "Comedy Italian Style" movement. This shift influenced directors like Pietro Germi with Divorce Italian Style (1961) and Mario Monicelli with Big Deal on Madonna Street (1958), who found ways to address social issues through comedy rather than drama.
